- When sentiment is high (≥0.6) and forecast shows a sharp upward spike, reduce the peak by 5–10% to avoid overreaction.  
- If sentiment is low (≤0.3) and forecast is trending up, cap the forecast at 1–2% above recent low to avoid false optimism.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if the last 3–5 days show strong mean reversion (price moving back toward 60–65), adjust forecast downward by 2–5% to reflect momentum.  
- When sentiment is volatile (fluctuating 0.3–0.6) and forecast is erratic, smooth transitions by averaging 2–3 prior values before projecting next.  
- If forecast overshoots true outcome by >3% in 3 consecutive days, apply a “lag correction” — reduce next forecast by 1–2% to account for delayed market reaction.  
- For sentiment history with high volatility (e.g., 0.1–0.3 then 0.6–0.7), assume model is overfitting — apply a 3–5% downward bias to forecast.  
- If true outcome is consistently 2–4% above forecast for 3+ days, assume model underestimates upward momentum — increase forecast by 1–3% for next 3 days.
